newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: SE Asian Grains-Malaysia buyers out on wheat rally.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grains-Malaysia buyers out on wheat rally.

text.p: Malaysian buyers are staying out the world wheat market following the steep run-up in Chicago futures prices to seven-month highs earlier this week on freezing spring weather in the U.S., traders said on Thursday. Elsewhere in the Southeast Asian grains and feeds market, Chinese corn continued to be actively offered, they added.

Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) wheat futures took a step back on Tuesday in a correction variously attributed to profit-taking on Monday's rally to the 20 cent-per-bushel trading limit and widely varying estimates of crop losses from the adverse weather.
CBOT May wheat futures were a touch firmer on the exchange's Project A after-hours trading system at 0530 GMT following a loss of 7-1/4 cents on the contract during open outcry on Tuesday.

But Malaysian traders said local flour mills were well covered over the next month or so and could afford to wait for the current U.S. wheat weather market to settle down. They said they were not concerned over a possible threat to supplies.
"Unless there's a downward correction in prices, buyers will stay out," an official at a Kuala Lumpur flour mill said.
But a trader said problems could emerge for Malaysia if serious damage to the U.S. spring wheat crop was confirmed, adding he expected prices to remain firm for some time.
"What is of more concern at the moment is the price," he said. "Given the high world wheat prices and that the price of wheat flour in Malaysia is regulated, there will be pressure on flour millers."
From March 16, the Malaysian government lowered the price of wheat flour to 1.0 ringgit a kg, compared with 1.10 ringgit previously, citing an increase in world output as the reason.

Imported "A" grade wheat in bags was quoted between 750 and 800 ringgit a tonne ex-factory/godown in Malaysia's central region, from 730 ringgit last week. "B" grade wheat was quoted around last week's 450 ringgit on the same basis.

Indonesian corn traders said they believed the U.S. corn market remained bullish, despite the retreat in the Chicago market overnight on confirmation Taiwan would cut back on its imports and some talk of an increase in U.S. sorghum acreage.
"The market is trading on technicals and not on fundamentals," one trader said. "Technicals are very bullish and the cold weather will certainly help firm sentiment."
They said the Indonesian market had been awash with offers of Chinese corn, which were competitively priced against South American offers.
"Chinese corn is being offered at US$148-$150 C&F compared with South American offers of $148 for Panamax shipments," one trader said. "Handy-sized shipments from South America were quoted at $158."
"Local feedmills are estimated to have purchased more than 120,000 tonnes of Chinese corn," he said.
The traders also said several local feedmills were well stocked with corn, while others were waiting for the arrival of imports which are expected to arrive through May.
Traders said local corn prices were generally stable at 405-410 rupiah a kg.
Domestic soymeal prices were also holding their ground at 830-840 rupiah a kg, while one trader said Indian soymeal was being offered at $342-$345 a tonne C&F.
In Malaysia, traders said they expected the arrival of Chinese corn at the end of the month, but that the volume was unlikely to be substantial.
The price of bulk corn ex-factory/godown in Malaysia's central region was quoted at between 420-430 ringgit a tonne C&F, against 410 ringgit a week earlier.
Soymeal averaged 885 ringgit for local material and 880 ringgit for imported product compared with 865 and 860 ringgit respectively last week.
